faq.title: F.A.Q. - How does it work?
faq.screenPlaceholder: Tap a question below and the professor will answer it up here.

items.q: How does the game work?
items.a: Buy a ticket. Once enough players join (or time runs out), the wheel closes and a winner is drawn on-chain. The winner doesn't get cash — they get the right to redeem their own USTC for USDC 1:1, up to the prize amount.

items.q: How is the winner picked?
items.a: Weighted by tickets: buying more improves your odds, but anyone with at least one ticket has a real chance. The pick happens entirely on-chain — the spinning wheel only reveals a result that's already decided, it never chooses it.

items.q: What happens if a round never fills up?
items.a: If the minimum number of players is never reached in time, the round expires and everyone who bought a ticket can reclaim their own money — no one has to ask for it back, it's a direct self-service transaction. It isn't unlimited, though: an expired round's unreclaimed ticket pool can be swept to the treasury once the app's own unclaimed-prize deadline passes, so don't let a reclaimable ticket sit unclaimed indefinitely.

items.q: Why does the countdown keep resetting?
items.a: Once the minimum number of players joins, every new ticket purchase extends the countdown a bit — like a live auction, so nobody gets shut out by a split-second timer. It can't extend forever though; there's a hard cap.

items.q: What does "on-chain and verifiable" mean?
items.a: Anyone can independently recompute the exact same result from public blockchain data, without taking our word for it. See "Verify this round" below any drawn round.

items.q: How is the winner obtained and verified on-chain?
items.a: In three separately-checkable steps. (1) The exact block where the draw happened has to be real — its height and its precise time. Anyone can open the raw block data (a link inside "Verify this round") and read it straight from the network, no app required. (2) The full list of everyone who bought a ticket has to be real too — it's also public on-chain data, with its own direct link in the same panel. (3) Both get fed into one fixed formula (a hash of the round, the block, and the ticket list together) that points to a single ticket. "Verify this round" runs all three steps live and shows every input it used, plus the resulting hash and both source links, in its "Show everything used in this calculation" section — you can hand that to anyone technical, or paste it to an AI, and ask them to redo the math themselves from scratch.

items.q: How do I know the app isn't just simulating the draw?
items.a: Because the check doesn't happen on our servers — it happens right in your own browser, which reaches out directly to Terra Classic's public network (not to Repeg Club) to fetch the block and the ticket list, then does the math itself. You can confirm this yourself: open your browser's developer tools while clicking "Verify on-chain" and you'll see the requests go out to the public network's own address, never to ours.

items.q: Is this actually decentralized, or could the team control the outcome?
items.a: The game, its prize, and its mechanics are decentralized and permissionless: every step, from start to payout, can be triggered by any wallet, not just ours. You don't have to trust our bot or our frontend either — "Verify this round" lets anyone recompute the draw from public blockchain data and get the same answer. The prize itself comes entirely from ticket sales, with no outside treasury the team controls. The one thing that still involves a team-held key is a limited admin power to move long-unclaimed funds to the treasury after a long timeout, so a forgotten prize or an abandoned round's pool doesn't sit lost forever inside the contract — it can never be redirected anywhere else, and the treasury itself requires 2-of-3 signers, not one person acting alone. And no, the team cannot control the outcome, and no one can.

items.q: Can one wallet buy all the tickets?
items.a: Every round has a fixed ticket cap per wallet: half of that round's maximum player capacity (minimum 1), no matter how many people actually end up joining. For example, a round that allows up to 10 players caps every wallet at 5 tickets. That's a hard ceiling on ticket count, not a live percentage guarantee — if only a couple of other players join, one wallet's tickets can still add up to more than half of that particular round's total (5 tickets out of 7 sold, say, if only two other wallets buy one each). The cap exists so nobody can buy an unlimited amount, not to promise an exact split. It cuts both ways, though: holding a bigger share means risking more of your own money on that round, and losing more if someone else wins — while a wallet with just one or two tickets risks very little and can multiply that small stake several times over if it wins. Bigger share, bigger risk; smaller share, bigger potential multiplier. That balance is what keeps the game fair even when a round doesn't fill evenly.

items.q: Does buying more tickets actually improve my odds?
items.a: Ticket count is exactly what decides the odds — never the wallet. The draw works over the full list of tickets bought (one entry per ticket, not one per wallet) and picks a single ticket from that list at random. So in a round with 7 tickets sold where one wallet holds 5 of them, that wallet has a 5-in-7 chance of winning — not a 1-in-3 chance just because only 3 wallets took part. You don't have to take our word for this either: open "Verify this round" on any drawn round and look at the ticket list inside "Show everything used in this calculation" — it lists one entry per ticket, in the exact order bought, duplicates included for wallets that bought more than one.

verify.copyJsonCaption: Everything above in one file: round ID, draw height/time, the full ticket list, the formula, the resulting hash, and both source links. Paste it anywhere — including to an AI — and ask it to redo the math.
verify.explanation: This app doesn't ask our own servers who won. When you click "Verify on-chain", your browser fetches the actual block straight from Terra Classic's public network and recomputes the winner itself, using the exact formula the smart contract runs: hash the round ID, that block's real height and time, and every ticket bought, then pick a ticket weighted by the result. Nobody chooses the outcome — the formula does, from data that didn't exist yet while the round was still open. If Repeg Club ever showed a different winner than what that formula actually produces, this check would fail instead of passing.

creatorTools.pageTitle: Create Your Own Luck with our Creator Tools

optionsGuide.title: Understand your options
optionsGuide.freeRaffleBullet1: Not creatable through this form yet — Single Winner/Podium here always require a paid ticket. Want free entry today? Use a free Airdrop instead (see below).
optionsGuide.freeRaffleBullet2: Once available: nobody risks money to enter — pure reach and marketing.
optionsGuide.freeRaffleBullet3: Once available: you don't earn revenue from it — you're giving the prize away.
optionsGuide.freeRaffleSuggestion: For now, a free Airdrop is the closest fit if your goal is building community or getting noticed without charging anyone.
optionsGuide.paidRaffleBullet1: Prize today: LUNC, USDC, or USTC only (more CW20 options coming as we whitelist them).
optionsGuide.paidRaffleBullet2: You set the ticket price and the prize — the gap between what's collected and the prize is your revenue (or your risk, if the prize costs more than ticket sales cover).
optionsGuide.paidRaffleBullet3: This form uses a 24h initial closing window once the minimum is reached (not yet creator-configurable) — a purchase in the final hour extends it by another hour, up to a 60-day hard cap — and canceling after paying the fee carries a penalty. Plan your marketing around that window before publishing.
optionsGuide.paidRaffleSuggestion: Ideal for fundraising: find the sweet spot between an attractive prize, an accessible ticket price, and enough time to market it.
optionsGuide.freeAirdropBullet1: Prize: LUNC, USDC, or USTC through this form today (CW20 support — including spreading your own token — exists on-chain but isn't exposed here yet).
optionsGuide.freeAirdropBullet2: Split equally among everyone who joins — there's no single winner.
optionsGuide.freeAirdropSuggestion: Ideal if your goal is getting a prize in front of more users — mass, whitelist-free distribution where everyone who joins for free gets a share.
optionsGuide.paidAirdropBullet1: If the worst-case per-wallet share would be worth less than the ticket price, you'll see a warning before funding — it extracts value from your community for nothing, and it's flagged publicly against your reputation as a creator.
optionsGuide.paidAirdropBullet2: That means the prize should scale with your expected audience — less about mass reach, more about a controlled distribution with fairness built in.
optionsGuide.paidAirdropSuggestion: Ideal if you want to charge an entry fee and give every participant a guaranteed share back — just make sure the prize is big enough for your expected audience, or you'll see a fairness warning before funding.
optionsGuide.allowlistBullet1: By default, any wallet can enter.
optionsGuide.allowlistBullet2: Add a list of specific wallets and only those can join — combine this with any of the 4 options above.
optionsGuide.allowlistSuggestion: Ideal if your goal is rewarding your existing community — for example, a snapshot of your token's holders — instead of opening it up to strangers.

faqWeekly.title: F.A.Q. - How does the weekly jackpot work?
faqWeekly.screenPlaceholder: Tap a question below and the professor will answer it up here.

items.q: How does the game work?
items.a: Buy a ticket. Once enough players join (or time runs out), the week closes and a winner is drawn on-chain. The winner doesn't get cash — they get the right to redeem their own USTC for USDC 1:1, up to the prize amount.

items.q: How is the winner picked?
items.a: Weighted by tickets: buying more improves your odds, but anyone with at least one ticket has a real chance. The pick happens entirely on-chain — the spinning wheel only reveals a result that's already decided, it never chooses it.

items.q: What happens if a week never fills up?
items.a: If the minimum number of players is never reached in time, the week expires and everyone who bought a ticket that week can reclaim their own money — no one has to ask for it back, it's a direct self-service transaction. It isn't unlimited, though: an expired week's unreclaimed ticket pool can be swept to the treasury once the app's own unclaimed-prize deadline passes, so don't let a reclaimable ticket sit unclaimed indefinitely.

items.q: Why doesn't the countdown reset the way Wheel of Repeg's does?
items.a: Weekly Round runs on one fixed countdown for the whole week (set the moment the week opens), not a rolling one that extends with every new ticket like Wheel of Repeg's rounds do. Once it hits zero, the week closes if enough players joined (or expires, with reclaimable tickets, if not) — buying late in the week doesn't buy anyone extra time.

items.q: Where does the weekly jackpot come from?
items.a: Two sources, shown separately in the pool breakdown above: this week's own ticket sales (the price rises daily, see below), plus a share automatically contributed on-chain every time a Wheel of Repeg round finishes and draws a winner, from that round's own ticket pool.

items.q: Why does the ticket price go up every day?
items.a: It rises by a fixed amount for each full day since the current week opened — not a percentage, a flat daily increment on top of the week's starting price. It resets back down to that starting price at the beginning of every new week.

items.q: If I buy a Wheel of Repeg ticket, am I automatically in the weekly jackpot too?
items.a: No — the two are separate draws with separate ticket pools. Every Wheel of Repeg round contributes part of its own proceeds to the weekly jackpot's pool automatically, but that doesn't give wheel players an entry into the weekly draw. You need your own Weekly Round ticket for a chance at this prize.

items.q: What does "on-chain and verifiable" mean?
items.a: Anyone can independently recompute the exact same result from public blockchain data, without taking our word for it. See "Verify this week" below any drawn week.

items.q: How is the winner obtained and verified on-chain?
items.a: In three separately-checkable steps. (1) The exact block where the draw happened has to be real — its height and its precise time. Anyone can open the raw block data (a link inside "Verify this week") and read it straight from the network, no app required. (2) The full list of everyone who bought a ticket that week has to be real too — it's also public on-chain data, with its own direct link in the same panel. (3) Both get fed into one fixed formula (a hash of the week, the block, and the ticket list together) that points to a single ticket. "Verify this week" runs all three steps live and shows every input it used, plus the resulting hash and both source links, in its "Show everything used in this calculation" section — you can hand that to anyone technical, or paste it to an AI, and ask them to redo the math themselves from scratch.

items.q: How do I know the app isn't just simulating the draw?
items.a: Because the check doesn't happen on our servers — it happens right in your own browser, which reaches out directly to Terra Classic's public network (not to Repeg Club) to fetch the block and the ticket list, then does the math itself. You can confirm this yourself: open your browser's developer tools while clicking "Verify on-chain" and you'll see the requests go out to the public network's own address, never to ours.

items.q: Is this actually decentralized, or could the team control the outcome?
items.a: The game, its prize, and its mechanics are decentralized and permissionless: every step, from start to payout, can be triggered by any wallet, not just ours. You don't have to trust our bot or our frontend either — "Verify this week" lets anyone recompute the draw from public blockchain data and get the same answer. The prize itself comes entirely from ticket sales, with no outside treasury the team controls. The one thing that still involves a team-held key is a limited admin power to move long-unclaimed funds to the treasury after a long timeout, so a forgotten prize or an abandoned week's pool doesn't sit lost forever inside the contract — it can never be redirected anywhere else, and the treasury itself requires 2-of-3 signers, not one person acting alone. And no, the team cannot control the outcome, and no one can.

items.q: Can one wallet buy all the tickets?
items.a: Every week has a fixed ticket cap per wallet: half of that week's maximum player capacity (minimum 1), no matter how many people actually end up joining. For example, a week that allows up to 10 players caps every wallet at 5 tickets. That's a hard ceiling on ticket count, not a live percentage guarantee — if only a couple of other players join, one wallet's tickets can still add up to more than half of that particular week's total (5 tickets out of 7 sold, say, if only two other wallets buy one each). The cap exists so nobody can buy an unlimited amount, not to promise an exact split. It cuts both ways, though: holding a bigger share means risking more of your own money on that week, and losing more if someone else wins — while a wallet with just one or two tickets risks very little and can multiply that small stake several times over if it wins. Bigger share, bigger risk; smaller share, bigger potential multiplier. That balance is what keeps the game fair even when a week doesn't fill evenly.

items.q: Does buying more tickets actually improve my odds?
items.a: Ticket count is exactly what decides the odds — never the wallet. The draw works over the full list of tickets bought that week (one entry per ticket, not one per wallet) and picks a single ticket from that list at random. So in a week with 7 tickets sold where one wallet holds 5 of them, that wallet has a 5-in-7 chance of winning — not a 1-in-3 chance just because only 3 wallets took part. You don't have to take our word for this either: open "Verify this week" on any drawn week and look at the ticket list inside "Show everything used in this calculation" — it lists one entry per ticket, in the exact order bought, duplicates included for wallets that bought more than one.

onrampFaq.title: F.A.Q. - How does getting USDC here work?
onrampFaq.screenPlaceholder: Tap a question below and the professor will answer it up here.

items.q: How does this actually work?
items.a: Pick which chain your funds are on (Noble, Cosmos Hub, or Osmosis), connect that wallet, and confirm. This project builds and asks you to sign the transfer itself, using Skip's routing to figure out any swap needed, then broadcasts it — your USDC lands directly in your own Terra Classic wallet.

items.q: What can I bring in?
items.a: USDC already sitting on Noble, Cosmos Hub, or Osmosis — or native ATOM or OSMO, which get swapped to USDC automatically along the way. You don't need to already hold USDC to use this.

items.q: How do I find my Noble wallet address?
items.a: If you already use Keplr, you likely already have one — just add Noble as a chain in Keplr's chain list (it isn't enabled by default) and it'll show you a Noble address for that same wallet, same seed phrase as your Terra Classic address. That's the address to withdraw USDC to from Binance/KuCoin if you're going that route.

items.q: Why only these chains — can't I bring something else?
items.a: This list is short on purpose. Every asset on it trades in deep, liquid markets, so the automatic swap doesn't lose real value to slippage. An obscure or illiquid token could get a bad swap on the way in — better to convert it to one of these first, somewhere else, than risk that here.

items.q: What about Bitcoin?
items.a: Not supported, and it's a real limitation, not an oversight: Skip Go (the router behind this tool) has no native Bitcoin chain at all — only wrapped representations like WBTC exist on other chains, and that isn't the same asset as real BTC sitting in a Bitcoin wallet. There's no way to bring BTC directly here today.

items.q: How much does it cost?
items.a: Depends on where you're coming from. Bringing USDC straight from Noble is cheapest — just a small fixed network fee, a few cents, plus Repeg Club's own 0.2% service fee on the amount. Coming from Cosmos Hub or Osmosis with native ATOM or OSMO adds a swap step with its own gas on top — still a small fraction of a typical amount, but worth knowing before sending something very small.

items.q: How long does it take?
items.a: Close to instant either way — Noble, Cosmos Hub, and Osmosis all settle directly on-chain, no bridge or long confirmation wait involved.

items.q: Is this safe — does Repeg Club hold my funds?
items.a: No. Funds move directly between your own wallets, on-chain, the same way the rest of this site already works with Keplr — Repeg Club never receives or holds anything in between. This project builds and asks you to sign the transfer itself, so you can always see exactly what you're signing — including the fee — before you confirm it in your wallet.

items.q: Why does my wallet show more than one message when I confirm?
items.a: For Noble, Cosmos Hub, and Osmosis, one signature covers both your transfer and Repeg Club's 0.2% service fee — that's why Keplr's confirmation screen shows 2 or 3 messages instead of just one. Nothing extra is being asked of you: it adds up to exactly the amount you typed, split between your transfer and the fee, both visible before you sign.

items.q: Why do I have to paste my Terra Classic address?
items.a: Terra Classic happens to use a different address format under the hood than the rest of the Cosmos chains here (Noble, Cosmos Hub, Osmosis) — so instead of guessing it, you paste it yourself, the same way you'd paste a destination address withdrawing from an exchange. Double-check it before sending — like any on-chain transfer, funds sent to the wrong address can't be recovered by Repeg Club.
